messages.content: You are an expert emergency medical dispatcher. Provide a concise, direct diagnosis and immediate action steps with no filler.
My neighbor's 3-year-old just pulled a pot of boiling soup off the stove onto herself. She's screaming and I can see large red patches and blisters forming across her chest and one arm.

Call 911 immediately. Gently remove any clothing that is not stuck to the burned skin. Run cool (not cold) water over the burned areas for at least 20 minutes. Do not apply ice, butter, or any ointment. Cover the burns loosely with a clean, non-stick cloth or cling wrap. Keep the child warm by covering unburned areas with a blanket to prevent hypothermia. Do not pop any blisters. Burns covering a large area of a child's body are life-threatening and require immediate hospital treatment.

I'm a camp counselor and one of our teenagers went swimming in the lake. He came out saying he feels dizzy and nauseous. Now he's having trouble breathing and his lips are turning blue. He was in the water about 30 minutes ago.

Call 911 immediately and mention possible secondary drowning. Have him sit upright to ease breathing. Monitor his breathing rate and consciousness closely. If his breathing stops or becomes very shallow, lay him on his back and begin rescue breathing. If he vomits, turn him on his side to keep the airway clear. Do not assume he is fine because he was walking and talking after leaving the water. Delayed respiratory distress after water aspiration can be fatal. He needs emergency medical evaluation and likely chest imaging and oxygen support.

I'm at home and my pregnant wife, who is 8 months along, just started having a severe headache, her vision is blurry, and her face and hands are very swollen. Her blood pressure monitor at home reads 165/110.

Call 911 immediately. This is consistent with preeclampsia or eclampsia, which is a life-threatening pregnancy emergency. Have her lie on her left side to improve blood flow. Keep the environment dim and quiet to reduce the risk of triggering a seizure. Do not give her any medications unless directed by a medical professional on the phone. If she begins seizing, protect her head, do not restrain her, and time the seizure. She needs emergency hospital evaluation for both her safety and the baby's safety.

We're hiking in the mountains at about 12,000 feet. My friend has a severe headache, keeps vomiting, and is now stumbling and confused. We started our hike from 8,000 feet this morning.

This is likely high altitude cerebral edema (HACE), which is life-threatening. Descend immediately, even if it is dark or difficult. Do not wait to see if symptoms improve. Aim to descend at least 2,000 to 3,000 feet as quickly as safely possible. If you have supplemental oxygen, administer it. If dexamethasone is in your medical kit, give 8mg immediately. Keep your friend warm, hydrated, and walking with close support. If he becomes unresponsive, place him in the recovery position and continue descending. Call for emergency evacuation if descent is not possible.

A coworker was using a nail gun and accidentally shot a nail into his upper thigh. The nail is still embedded and there's blood slowly oozing around it. He's conscious and in a lot of pain.

Call 911 immediately. Do not attempt to remove the nail. Removing an embedded object can cause uncontrolled bleeding if it has punctured a major blood vessel. Stabilize the nail in place by packing clean cloths or gauze around its base so it cannot shift or move. Have the worker lie down and keep still. Monitor for signs of heavy bleeding or shock, including pale skin, rapid pulse, dizziness, or confusion. Keep him calm and warm until paramedics arrive. The upper thigh contains the femoral artery, so this wound has the potential to become rapidly life-threatening if the object is disturbed.
